[00:58:04] building off of DeepSeek R1 and also Kimi.

[00:58:16] are actually quite interesting.

[00:58:20] is they mix thinking and non-thinking things with tags.
[00:58:24] And that's how they end up having a thinking mode, where
[00:58:28] the model has a long COT and they can mix
[00:58:31] that with a non-thinking mode.

[00:58:46] I thought this was quite interesting,
[00:58:49] which is they have this way of early exiting thinking where
[00:58:52] if they append a special string, they'll immediately stop the COT
[00:58:56] and the model is forced to give an answer to whatever prompt
[00:59:00] is given.

[00:59:05] like ChatGPT, where you're able to terminate the thinking early
[00:59:09] and try to get an immediate answer, for example.
[00:59:12] But what we see with this and I've always
[00:59:16] thought this was a surprising an interesting thing, which
[00:59:19] is that as you vary the thinking budget, doing
[00:59:22] this early termination trick, you end up
[00:59:25] finding that the performance of the model
[00:59:29] degrades gracefully, even though at the lower-thinking budgets,

[00:59:38] responses even at that point.
[00:59:41] And we see that consistently, even
[00:59:42] with very small-thinking budgets, the thinking
[00:59:44] mode models are much better on all
[00:59:46] of these mathematical or coding tasks
[00:59:49] compared to the instant response mode, which

[00:59:52] is much more of the classic instruction following plus RLHF
[00:59:57] models.
[01:00:01] And so you can-- one of the nice things they do for us is look
[01:00:05] at the contribution of all of the different components
[01:00:08] to performance.
[01:00:09] And in many ways, this is not something that
[01:00:11] should surprise you too much.
[01:00:14] If you do this reasoning RL and then general RL,
[01:00:19] you're able to slowly get improvements
[01:00:22] in all of the different tasks, things like Arena-Hard
[01:00:25] or CounterFactQA.

[01:00:30] and we see significant boosts to that performance
[01:00:33] across the board.
[01:00:34] There are some degradations that we see in math and coding
[01:00:37] because we fuse together non-thinking components,
[01:00:41] but the degradation is not so bad.

[01:00:46] in an absolute sense are small in later releases,
[01:00:50] I think in some of the Qwen 3.5, they've
[01:00:53] gone back on fusing both thinking
[01:00:54] and non-thinking into a single model.
[01:00:57] I think what-- they used to call this hybrid models because they
[01:01:00] found this drop unacceptable.
[01:01:02] They wanted to squeeze out all the juice
[01:01:04] possible on thinking modes.
[01:01:06] And so they've now, I think, separated
[01:01:08] these models from each other.
[01:01:11] The very last topic and paper that I want to cover is Qwen 3--
[01:01:20] or sorry, I flipped the two.
[01:01:21] It's Coder-Next not Next-Coder, which is one of the newer models
[01:01:26] to come out.
[01:01:27] And I think if you're interested in general agent
[01:01:29] stuff, of course, there's other agents things
[01:01:31] to think about harnesses.
[01:01:33] But if you're interested in how do you actually build an agent.
[01:01:35] This is probably a good report to go read.
[01:01:38] Qwen3-Coder-Next great agent post-training paper.
[01:01:44] But in some ways, post-training for an agent
[01:01:46] is not very different from everything that we've described.
[01:01:49] It's not like there's a new agent training algorithm.
[01:01:52] Really, you should internalize this lesson
[01:01:55] throughout the entire class.
[01:01:56] Data is the important thing.
[01:01:58] So if you're going to train an agent or post-training an agent,
[01:02:01] what are you going to do?
[01:02:02] You're going to get the data together.
[01:02:04] So there's two parts to the data.
[01:02:06] To get a lot of the capabilities,
[01:02:08] you can't just inject them at the end.
[01:02:11] You have to probably start a little bit earlier.
[01:02:13] And so there's an extensive mid-training phase
[01:02:15] that happens to try to get as much coding
[01:02:18] and agent like capabilities into the model as possible.
[01:02:22] So they'll do things like they'll
[01:02:23] take repositories and concatenate the files
[01:02:26] in the repository to generate these very long context data
[01:02:29] and put it into the model.
[01:02:30] We know that the model is eventually
[01:02:32] going to see these very long COT traces, where
[01:02:34] maybe the agent has opened a bunch of files, very

[01:02:43] try to construct synthetic context for it,
[01:02:45] using RAG that is potentially helpful for understanding
[01:02:48] the pull request.

[01:03:45] collection procedure to try to get
[01:03:47] some of these agentic abilities into mid training.
[01:03:50] And then the Qwen folks do something
[01:03:53] that I don't know if I've seen before.

[01:04:27] V3.5, sorry, DeepSeek V3.5 or 3.2.

[01:06:17] talking about, the reason why we can put more and more compute
[01:06:21] into RL is because we believe that our reward
